section.title: You Will Not Abandon My Soul
section.sectionRationale: One of the Psalter's most explicitly messianic texts, quoted at length by Peter at Pentecost and by Paul at Pisidian Antioch as direct prophecy of Christ's resurrection. David voices a settled security in God as his whole portion, and his closing confidence that God will not abandon him to Sheol reaches beyond what David's own body experienced, pointing to the Holy One who would not see decay.
section.thesis: David's confession that the Lord is his only good and his secure portion rises, in its final verses, to a hope beyond his own grave, a hope the apostles show is fulfilled only in the bodily resurrection of Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: David's refuge and the delight he takes in the saints rather than false gods; the Lord as his chosen portion and secure inheritance; his confidence that God is always before him so he will not be shaken; and the climactic hope that God will not abandon his soul to Sheol, fulfilled in Christ's resurrection.

units.label: Apart from You I have no good thing
units.note: refuge and delight in the saints

verses.text: Preserve me, O God, for in You I take {{chasah|refuge}}.
I said to the LORD, “You are my Lord; apart from You I have no good thing.”

As for the saints in the land, they are the excellence 
in whom all my delight resides.
Sorrows will multiply to those who chase other gods. I will not pour out their libations of blood, or speak their names with my lips.

units.label: The Lord is my chosen portion

verses.text: The LORD is my chosen {{cheleq|portion}} and my cup; You have made my lot secure.
The lines of my boundary have fallen in pleasant places; surely my inheritance is delightful.
I will bless the LORD who counsels me; even at night my conscience instructs me.
I have set the LORD always before me. Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken.
Therefore my heart is glad and my tongue rejoices; my body also will dwell securely.

units.label: You will not abandon my soul to Sheol

verses.text: For You will not abandon my soul to {{sheol|Sheol}}, nor will You let Your {{chasid|Holy One}} see decay.

You have made known to me the path of life; You will fill me with joy in Your presence, 
with eternal pleasures at Your right hand.

chasah.gloss: To take refuge, seek shelter, flee for protection. David opens the psalm by casting himself on God as his only place of safety, the same posture of trust that runs through the whole psalm's confidence.

cheleq.gloss: Portion, share, allotted inheritance, drawn from the language of Israel's tribal land divisions. David says the LORD Himself, not a plot of ground, is his cheleq, the secure share that defines his whole life.

sheol.gloss: The realm of the dead, the grave, the place of departed spirits in Old Testament thought. David's confidence that God will not abandon him to Sheol reaches for a hope beyond death itself, one the New Testament shows fulfilled in resurrection.

chasid.gloss: Holy One, godly one, one marked by covenant loyalty and faithfulness. Peter and Paul both apply this title in verse 10 directly to Jesus Christ, whose body, unlike David's, never saw decay, since He rose bodily from the dead.

basic.context: David opens by casting himself entirely on God for refuge, delighting in God's people rather than in idols. He then declares that the Lord Himself, not land or wealth, is his chosen portion and secure inheritance. Because he keeps the Lord always before him, he will not be shaken, and his confidence rises to its highest point in the final verses: God will not abandon his soul to the grave, nor let His Holy One see decay, and he will know the fullness of joy in God's presence forever.
basic.hermeneutics: David wrote this psalm from his own experience of trust in God, and in one sense it does describe his own settled hope. But the apostles Peter and Paul both insist, quoting verse 10 directly, that its ultimate fulfillment goes beyond David: David himself died and was buried and his body did see decay, so this verse points forward, as genuine prophecy, to the resurrection of great David's greater Son, Jesus Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: David chasah, takes refuge, in God alone, and calls the LORD his cheleq, portion, the secure share that replaces any claim to land or wealth. His climactic hope is that God will not abandon him to sheol, the realm of the dead, nor let His chasid, Holy One, see decay, language the apostles apply directly to Christ's bodily resurrection.
basic.typology: David, God's anointed king, functions here as a type of the greater Anointed One, Christ, whose body alone truly never saw decay; David's own hope in this psalm reaches further than his own experience could fulfill, anticipating the resurrection accomplished in Jesus.
basic.christ: In Acts 2:25-31, Peter preaches at Pentecost that David could not have been speaking only of himself in verse 10, since David's tomb was in Jerusalem to that very day; David, as a prophet, spoke of the resurrection of the Christ. Paul repeats this same argument in Acts 13:35-37 at Pisidian Antioch, declaring that Jesus, unlike David, saw no decay because God raised Him from the dead.
basic.god: God is shown as the sole sufficient good, the secure portion, and counselor who guides even in the night, and ultimately as the One whose faithfulness reaches beyond death itself, refusing to abandon His Holy One to the grave.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 2:25-31 is Peter's Pentecost sermon quoting this psalm as prophecy of Christ's resurrection. Acts 13:35-37 is Paul's parallel argument at Pisidian Antioch. Hebrews 2:11-13 shows Christ delighting in His people much as David delights in the saints.
basic.oneStory: David's confession that God alone is his portion and refuge rises to a hope beyond his own grave, a hope the whole rest of the story shows was never meant for David alone but for the greater Son of David, Jesus Christ, whose resurrection secures eternal joy in God's presence for everyone who trusts in Him.

context.literary:
Psalm 16 is a psalm of confession in the first person, and it moves in a rising line from the cramped and defensive to the open and unlimited. It begins with a request, 'Preserve me,' and a reason, 'in You I take refuge.' It ends with 'eternal pleasures at Your right hand.' In between, the psalm keeps changing its picture of what God is to David. In verse 1 He is a refuge, in verse 2 the only good, in verses 5 and 6 a portion, a cup, a lot and a piece of ground, in verse 7 a counsellor, in verse 8 a presence at David's right hand, and in verses 10 and 11 the one who holds back the grave and shows the path of life. The images pile up until they cover the whole of life, and then the last two verses carry the sequence past death.

The psalm also turns on a series of contrasts between two ways to live. Verse 4 sets 'those who chase other gods' against the psalmist's refusal to name their names; verses 5 and 6 set an inheritance in the LORD against any other lot. The negative in verse 4 is short and sharp, and the rest of the psalm is positive, so that the shadow is small next to the light.

The Hebrew title calls this a miktam, a word the BSB footnote says is probably a musical or liturgical term, used of Psalms 16 and 56 to 60. Its meaning is not known with certainty, and the discussion should not be pressed.

There is a sense of 'therefore' running through the closing verses. 'Because He is at my right hand, I will not be shaken. Therefore my heart is glad ... For You will not abandon my soul to Sheol.' Each claim is grounded in the one before, so that the resurrection hope of verse 10 is the end of a reasoned trust and not an isolated leap. The psalm runs from what David has said to the LORD in verse 2, to what he has decided in verse 8, to what he expects in verse 10.
context.historical:
The title again gives David as author, without a named occasion. The psalm's first four verses have a religious edge. In a land surrounded by peoples who worshiped other gods, and in a time when Israel itself often slid into their practices, the psalmist declares where his loyalty lies. The 'libations of blood' of verse 4 are offerings poured out in the worship of other gods, and the refusal even to speak their names echoes the command, 'You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips,' Exodus 23:13. Psalm 106:37-38 recalls how far such worship could go, with children sacrificed and the land polluted with blood.

The language of 'portion', 'lot' and 'boundary lines' in verses 5 and 6 comes from the division of the land. When Joshua had the country mapped out, he 'cast lots' for each tribe in the LORD's presence, Joshua 18:6, and each family received its share by boundary lines. The tribe of Levi was the exception. The priests and Levites had no land, because 'the LORD is their inheritance,' Deuteronomy 18:1-2, and God told Aaron, 'I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites,' Numbers 18:20. David, a king and no Levite, takes to himself the priestly confession: whatever land or wealth he has, his true holding is the LORD.

The fear of Sheol belongs to the Old Testament's view of death as a place of silence and darkness, as Psalm 6:5 says. Faith in a life beyond it was not yet fully spelled out, though a number of texts push toward it, Psalm 49:15, Psalm 73:24 and, later, Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2. David lived under a promise that his house would endure, and Peter, standing in Jerusalem centuries later, could point to the fact that David's tomb was still there, Acts 2:29. The psalm's hope, then, was voiced in a period when believers were stretching toward the resurrection without a full description of it.
context.canonical:
Psalm 16 is one of the most heavily used psalms in the New Testament, and it is quoted in the two great missionary sermons of Acts, both of which turn on the resurrection. In Acts 2:25-31 Peter quotes verses 8 to 11 at Pentecost, arguing that David 'was a prophet' and that 'foreseeing this, David spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay,' Acts 2:30-31. In Acts 13:35-37 Paul cites verse 10 at Pisidian Antioch, joining it to another text, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David,' Acts 13:34. The two quotations share the Greek word for 'holy', which is how Paul links them. He then draws the same conclusion Peter did: David 'fell asleep. His body was buried with his fathers and saw decay. But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay,' Acts 13:36-37.

The psalm's theme of the LORD as a portion runs through the canon: Psalm 73:26, 'God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever'; Psalm 119:57, 'The LORD is my portion'; Psalm 142:5; and Lamentations 3:24, 'The LORD is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in Him.' The hope of rescue from Sheol resonates with Psalm 49:15, Hosea 13:14 and Job's confession that in his flesh he will see God, Job 19:25-27. In the New Testament it grows into the hope that 'God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him,' 1 Thessalonians 4:14, and 'By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also,' 1 Corinthians 6:14. The last line of the psalm is answered in 1 John 3:2 and in the vision of the Lamb's people who will see His face.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David meant this psalm as a settled statement of allegiance, and he meant his people to sing it. The opening verses declare, against every rival, that the LORD is the only good he has and the only refuge he will use. The middle of the psalm tells the hearer what that allegiance means for ordinary life: delight in God's people, refusal of other gods, contentment with the lot he has been given, and a habit of keeping God before him at every hour, even at night. The point for the first hearers was that faith is a choice of portion. It is one thing to say 'the LORD is my God' and another to say that He is what I have, in place of anything else I could have had.

The psalm also expresses a bold hope. David expects that God will not leave him to the grave, and he expects to know the path of life and the joy of God's presence. What he understood of his own words cannot be measured. What he plainly meant was that the God who was his portion in life would not stop being his portion at death, and he wanted Israel to have the same confidence.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes David's own confession. It is not a promise given to every believer in the same words, and it does not say that a believer will never suffer, since the language of refuge and preservation assumes that danger is near. What it prescribes, by the example of its form, is the posture: to name the LORD as one's good, to treat His people as the ones in whom one delights, to refuse other gods, and to keep Him always in view.

Verse 10 needs separate handling. The apostles read it as a specific prophecy of Christ's resurrection, and that reading is authoritative for Christians. It should not be turned into a promise that a believer's body will never die or decay. The believer shares in the resurrection hope through Christ, who is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and not by escaping the grave as Christ did. The psalm's other verses, on refuge, portion and joy, can be prayed by any believer, while verse 10 is prayed with the recognition that its fullest meaning belongs to Jesus.

debates.question: Did David understand himself to be prophesying the Messiah's resurrection in verse 10?

views.label: David spoke better than he knew, uttering a genuine prophecy of Christ's resurrection
views.case: Peter says plainly that David 'was a prophet' who, 'foreseeing this,' spoke of the resurrection of the Christ, Acts 2:30-31. On this reading the Spirit gave David words whose full meaning he only partly grasped, and the apostolic reading is the historic Christian one.

views.label: David expressed confidence about his own life, and the apostles show a fuller sense in Christ
views.case: The psalm's language of refuge, portion and security fits David's own circumstances, and 'abandon my soul to Sheol' can mean being spared an untimely death. The fuller meaning appears only in the light of the resurrection, a pattern sometimes called a fuller sense intended by the divine author.

views.label: An argument from a lesser to a greater case
views.case: Paul and Peter both argue that whatever David meant, his body did see decay, Acts 2:29 and Acts 13:36, so the words cannot have been fully true of him. On this view the apostles are showing that the promise only holds without remainder in one who did not decay, without deciding what David consciously foresaw.

debates.bearing: All three views agree with the apostles on the result, that verse 10 finds its complete truth in the resurrection of Jesus. They differ on how much David knew, and the text of Acts leaves that question partly open.

debates.question: Who are 'the saints in the land' of verse 3, and how does it connect with verse 4?

views.label: God's faithful people, in whom David delights
views.case: Most English versions, including the BSB, read verse 3 as praise of the godly. It fits the way the psalm sets delight in God's people against the pull of idolatry, and Psalm 4:3 speaks of the LORD setting 'apart the godly for Himself.'

views.label: Spirit-beings or gods worshiped in the land, whom David rejects
views.case: The Hebrew of verses 2 and 3 is difficult, and some interpreters take 'the holy ones' as the powers the nations honoured, reading the verse as a rejection that leads into verse 4. On that reading the sentence is a contrast with the LORD and not praise of people.

debates.bearing: The text is hard, and the bearing is the same on both readings: the LORD alone is David's good. The first reading gives the psalm a communal warmth that fits the New Testament's picture of the church as those in whom Christ takes delight.

debates.question: Does the word in verse 10 mean 'pit' or 'decay'?

views.label: Decay, as the Greek Old Testament and Acts read it
views.case: The Septuagint translated the word as 'corruption', and Peter and Paul both use the sense of decay, Acts 2:31 and Acts 13:37. The argument that David's body saw decay while Christ's did not depends on that meaning.

views.label: Pit, the grave itself
views.case: The Hebrew noun can be derived from a root meaning 'pit', as in Psalm 9:15 and Psalm 30:3, and some modern translators prefer it. On that reading David hopes not to go down to the grave, and the parallel with Sheol is tighter.

debates.bearing: Either derivation supports the resurrection hope, since not seeing the pit and not seeing decay both mean not being held by death. The apostles' Greek text makes the point about David's tomb sharper.

study.originalLanguages:
The plea of verse 1, 'Preserve me,' uses the verb shamar, to guard or keep, the word used of a watchman, a shepherd or a keeper of a garden. It is followed by a perfect verb, 'I have taken refuge,' which speaks of a decision already made. David asks for what he has already chosen to rely on. In verse 2, 'apart from You I have no good thing' is literally close to 'my good is not beyond You.' It says that nothing David counts as good lies outside God, not that God is one good among others.

Verse 7 says that 'even at night my conscience instructs me.' The BSB footnote points out that the Hebrew reads 'my kidneys instruct me.' In Hebrew thought the kidneys are the seat of the deepest feelings and moral sense, and God is said to test them, Psalm 7:9 and Psalm 73:21. The verb 'instructs' is one that means to discipline or train, as a father corrects a child. The night is when a person is alone with himself, and David says even then the LORD is teaching him from the inside.

In verse 8 the verb 'I have set' is a form of the ordinary verb for placing or putting, and it describes a deliberate act. The same verse in the Septuagint reads 'I foresaw the Lord always before me,' as the BSB footnote records, and this is the form Peter quotes in Acts 2:25, 'I saw the Lord always before me.' The change from 'set' to 'saw' or 'foresaw' is small in Greek, and it is what allows Peter to hear David as someone looking ahead, not merely someone keeping God in mind. The verse ends with the same verb as Psalm 15:5, 'I will not be shaken.'

The most discussed word is the one in verse 10 that the BSB renders 'decay.' The Hebrew shachat can come from a root meaning 'pit', as in Psalm 9:15 and Psalm 30:3, or from a root meaning to corrupt, which is the sense the Septuagint chose when it translated it with a Greek word for corruption or decay, and it is the Greek word Peter and Paul rely on. The debate is real, and either way the verse is about not being held by death.

Verse 11 has 'the path of life', a phrase found also in Proverbs 15:24, 'The path of life leads upward for the wise, that he may avoid going down to Sheol.' The verse ends with two words of fullness. The first is a word that describes satisfaction to the full, the word behind 'fill you with joy,' which in Psalm 17:15 says, 'when I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence.' The second is a word for what lasts, the word behind 'eternal', which stands at the end of the verse and closes the psalm.

Finally, 'the lines of my boundary' in verse 6 is literally 'lines' or 'ropes', the measuring cords that marked out a family's share of land. David uses the surveyor's word for the LORD's gift, so that the pleasant places are not scenery but an allotted inheritance.

typology.type: David, the anointed king whose hope outruns his tomb
typology.fulfillment: David speaks as God's anointed of a deliverance that he himself did not receive. Peter points out that 'the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day,' Acts 2:29, and that David 'was a prophet,' Acts 2:30. The king's confidence therefore reaches past his own life to his greater descendant, the one God promised to place on his throne. The correspondence is between the king who trusts and the King who is raised; the type falls short because David's body decayed, Acts 13:36, while the Son of David 'did not see decay,' Acts 13:37.

typology.type: The LORD as portion, like the Levites
typology.fulfillment: The tribe of Levi had no land, because the LORD was their inheritance, Deuteronomy 18:1-2, and David takes the words for himself. In Christ the whole people of God enter that state: believers are chosen as God's own in Him, Ephesians 1:11, and have been qualified 'to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light,' Colossians 1:12, an inheritance 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,' 1 Peter 1:3-4. The correspondence is a life whose real holding is God Himself; the escalation is that it is opened to all who are in Christ. The type falls short because the Levites' portion was mediated by the temple, while ours is held in Christ.

typology.type: The cup that is my portion
typology.fulfillment: David calls the LORD his 'portion and my cup', a cup of blessing. Christ took a different cup in Gethsemane: 'Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will,' Mark 14:36. He drank what was ours so that what is left for His people is what Psalm 116:13 calls 'the cup of salvation.' The pattern is a cup that comes from God's hand, and the escalation is that Christ receives the bitter one so the believer may receive the sweet. The type falls short because David's cup was a gift; Christ's cost His life.

typology.type: The right hand and the path of life
typology.fulfillment: David hopes to know the path of life and pleasures 'at Your right hand.' Peter finishes his argument by saying that Jesus, 'exalted ... to the right hand of God,' Acts 2:33, has taken that place, and he ties it to Psalm 110:1 in Acts 2:34-35. The Letter to the Hebrews adds that Christ endured the cross 'for the joy set before Him' and then 'sat down at the right hand of the throne of God,' Hebrews 12:2. What David longed for as a hope, Christ enters as a fact. The correspondence is real; the type falls short because David asked to share God's presence, while Christ shares God's throne.

David expects God not to leave his soul in Sheol. The resurrection of Christ is the pattern that fills this out: He was buried and 'raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:3-4, and it was 'impossible for Him to be held in its clutches,' Acts 2:24. Hosea's word, 'I will ransom them from the power of Sheol,' Hosea 13:14, and Christ's own, 'I hold the keys of Death and of Hades,' Revelation 1:18, show the escalation. The type falls short because David hoped for rescue, and Christ actually passed through death and came out the other side, first among many.

study.christ:
Psalm 16 is one of the few Old Testament passages the New Testament quotes at length, and it treats it as a witness to Christ's resurrection. That gives this study a firmer footing than most: the link does not depend on a reader's imagination but on what the apostles said.

Peter's sermon at Pentecost is the fullest use. After announcing that God raised Jesus, 'releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches,' Acts 2:24, he quotes Psalm 16:8-11 and then reasons from it. 'Brothers, I can tell you with confidence that the patriarch David died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. But he was a prophet and knew that God had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne. Foreseeing this, David spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that He was not abandoned to Hades, nor did His body see decay,' Acts 2:29-31. The argument is that the psalm could not have been fully true of David, whose tomb was known, and that it was fully true of the Son of David.

Paul makes the same point at Pisidian Antioch. He pairs Psalm 16:10 with the promise 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David,' Acts 13:34, and concludes that David 'fell asleep. His body was buried with his fathers and saw decay. But the One whom God raised from the dead did not see decay,' Acts 13:36-37. He finds a link in the word 'holy' that appears in both texts. Notice how the resurrection here is not a mere miracle but the keeping of the covenant promise to David: God's fidelity to His anointed line is the reason the Holy One is not left in the grave.

The psalm also gives words for Christ's inner life, though the New Testament does not put them in His mouth. He kept the LORD before Him always and was not shaken, from the wilderness to Gethsemane, and He endured the cross 'for the joy set before Him,' Hebrews 12:2. The 'path of life' and the 'pleasures at Your right hand' are what He entered when 'He sat down at the right hand of the throne of God,' Hebrews 12:2, and He is the one through whom His people will follow, since 'God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him,' 1 Thessalonians 4:14. Paul ties the person and the hope together: 'that I may gain Christ,' Philippians 3:8. The person who says 'the LORD is my portion' finds that the portion is a person.

The risen Lord Himself told His disciples that 'everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms,' Luke 24:44. It is fair to say Psalm 16 was among the psalms He had in mind, though the text does not say which ones He named.

There is a limit to the reading. Not every phrase of the psalm is about Jesus, and the language of refuge, delight and boundary lines belongs to David's own devotion. The apostles' claim is tied to verses 8 to 11, and above all to verse 10.
study.god:
Psalm 16 shows God as the sufficient good. David does not say that God is one among the good things in his life; he says, 'apart from You I have no good thing.' Everything else he enjoys, the saints, the land, the pleasant places, is received as a gift from Him, in line with James 1:17, 'Every good and perfect gift is from above.' The psalm's picture of God is a giver who is Himself the best of His gifts, and Psalm 84:11 says the same, 'He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity.'

He is a refuge who actually keeps. David's request 'Preserve me' is met in the confidence of the whole psalm, and elsewhere the refuge is described as the shelter of His wings, Psalm 57:1 and Psalm 91:4. God's protection is real and personal.

He is a counsellor who works from within. 'I will bless the LORD who counsels me; even at night my conscience instructs me.' The Hebrew has David's inner being trained by God in the dark hours. That is a God who does not merely give commands from outside but forms His people's desires. The psalm links it with the practice of keeping Him 'always before me', and with the promise that He is at David's right hand, the place of an advocate or defender.

He is the God of the covenant lot. The language of portion, lot and boundary lines is the language of a landowner giving inheritances, and David says the LORD has made his 'lot secure.' God is the one who keeps what He has apportioned. This is why David can call his inheritance delightful, and why the psalm has no anxiety over what has been left to others.

Most strikingly, He is the God who is stronger than death. The psalm's confidence that He 'will not abandon my soul to Sheol' shows a God whose faithfulness does not stop at the grave. Psalm 139:7-10 says that even in Sheol He is present, and Hosea 13:14 gives His own word, 'I will ransom them from the power of Sheol.' The psalm holds this together with the reality that David will die; the God who keeps His people does so through death and not always around it. The apostles read it as fulfilled at the point where He raised His Holy One, Acts 2:24, and the hope of His people rests on the same act, 1 Corinthians 6:14.

He is a God of joy. The psalm ends with 'fullness of joy' and 'eternal pleasures.' The God of Scripture is not a dour master who tolerates our happiness; He is its source and its end. Worship, as this psalm teaches it, is not the duty of those who have nothing better, but the delight of those who have found the best thing there is.

For worship, the psalm teaches contentment and courage together: contentment with a lot God has given, and courage to look at death and say, with the apostles' help, that God will not leave His Holy One there, nor those who are His.

crossReferences.note: Peter's Pentecost sermon quotes verses 8 to 11 and reasons that David, whose tomb was known, was speaking as a prophet of the resurrection of the Christ. It is the plainest apostolic reading of the psalm.

Paul joins Psalm 16:10 to the promise of 'the holy and sure blessings promised to David,' and argues that David's body saw decay while the One God raised did not. It confirms that the resurrection was the keeping of a covenant promise.

'I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites.' God's word to Aaron is the background of David's 'The LORD is my chosen portion.' It shows the priestly meaning of having the LORD Himself as one's holding.

The Levites 'shall have no portion or inheritance with Israel ... the LORD is their inheritance.' It repeats the point with the sacrifices as the priest's share, and helps show why a king who says the LORD is his portion is claiming something unusual.

Joshua says he will cast lots for the tribes 'in the presence of the LORD.' It gives the setting for the 'lot' and 'boundary' language of verses 5 and 6, where David treats his inheritance as assigned by God's own hand.
'You must not invoke the names of other gods; they must not be heard on your lips.' It stands behind David's refusal in verse 4 to speak the names of the gods of those who chase them.

Another portion psalm: 'You hold my right hand,' and 'God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever.' It shares the right hand, the counsel and the hope of being received in glory, and it places the same confidence beyond the flesh's failing.

'But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself.' It shows that the hope of Psalm 16:10 was not a lone expression, and that Israel's worshipers were reaching for a rescue from the grave.
'When I awake, I will be satisfied in Your presence.' It answers Psalm 16:11's 'fill you with joy in Your presence' with the same picture of the sleeper waking to see God's face.

'Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.' Peter pairs it with Psalm 16 in Acts 2:34-35, since both speak of the right hand and both are about a Son of David who is more than David.

'He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures.' Paul says the resurrection is 'of first importance' and rests on Scripture, and Psalm 16 is one of the texts the apostles used to show it.

'A living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading.' It joins the psalm's two themes, inheritance and resurrection, and applies them to every believer.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 16 sits at a turning point in the story between the fall and the promise. Since Genesis 3, death has been the enemy the whole Bible reckons with, and the account of Adam ends with 'and then he died,' Genesis 5:5. The Old Testament faithful knew that death was real and dreaded it. Yet a line of texts reaches beyond it, and Psalm 16 is among the boldest: God will not leave His faithful one in Sheol, and there is a path of life ahead.

The psalm also answers a question that runs through the story of the land. Israel was promised an inheritance, and each tribe received its lines and lot. But the deepest inheritance in the story was never a piece of ground. It was God Himself, given first to the Levites and here confessed by a king. In the exile, when the land was lost, that confession was the only holding that could not be taken. The people who returned did so with the sense that the LORD had always been the real portion.

The psalm sets up the Gospels' greatest claim. A descendant of David would not see decay, and Peter's sermon says that Jesus is that descendant. The resurrection is the hinge of the whole Bible: 'Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures ... He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:3-4. Psalm 16 is one of the Scriptures that opens the way, showing that the resurrection was not a surprise to the God of Israel but the completion of a promise.

The story then widens to everyone who is in Christ. The believer's inheritance is 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,' 1 Peter 1:3-4, and death is no longer the last word but a sleep from which God will bring His people with Jesus, 1 Thessalonians 4:14.

The new creation is the place where the psalm's last line comes true. 'Fullness of joy' and 'eternal pleasures' become the life of a people who see God's face, 1 John 3:2, and the dwelling of God is with them, Revelation 21:3. The ground given to the tribes gives way to the inheritance that David called delightful, the LORD Himself, whom no one is asked to leave.

sermon.title: Prayer for Security
sermon.why: Keller preaches this psalm as the very text Peter used in the first Christian sermon at Pentecost, tracing how David's cry for an unshakeable refuge is answered fully only in the risen Christ.

quiz.q: What does David declare in verse 2 about his relationship to God?

options.text: That the LORD is his Lord, and apart from Him he has no good thing.
options.note: This is David's direct confession of total dependence on God as his sole good.

options.text: That he has many good things apart from God that still bring him joy.
options.note: This directly contradicts David's stated confession in verse 2.

options.text: That other gods provide some lesser but real good things.
options.note: David explicitly rejects other gods in verse 4, warning that sorrows multiply for those who chase them.

options.text: That good things come primarily from his own wisdom and effort.
options.note: This shifts credit away from God as the sole source, which is the opposite of what David confesses.

quiz.q: What does David mean by calling the LORD his 'portion' in verse 5?

options.text: That God Himself, not land or wealth, is his secure and chosen inheritance.
options.note: This draws on the language of Israel's tribal land divisions, applying it to God Himself as David's true inheritance.

options.text: That God has given him a specific plot of land in Israel.
options.note: The psalm uses inheritance language metaphorically for God Himself, not a literal land grant.

options.text: That his financial portion is secured through wise investment.
options.note: The psalm concerns spiritual security in God, not financial planning.

options.text: That he shares his portion equally among his household.
options.note: This misses the point that the portion described is God Himself, not a distributed inheritance.

quiz.q: How does Peter use Psalm 16:10 in his Pentecost sermon in Acts 2?

options.text: He argues that David, as a prophet, foresaw and spoke of the resurrection of the Christ, since David's own body remained in the tomb and saw decay.
options.note: This is Peter's exact argument in Acts 2:25-31, central to the first Christian sermon.

options.text: He argues that David's own body was miraculously preserved from decay.
options.note: Peter explicitly states the opposite, that David's tomb was still present and his body did see decay.

options.text: He uses it only as a general example of Old Testament poetry.
options.note: Peter's use is a specific theological argument for Christ's resurrection, not merely a poetic illustration.

options.text: He applies it to the future resurrection of all believers only, not to Jesus specifically.
options.note: Peter's argument centers specifically on Jesus's own resurrection as the fulfillment, though it has implications for believers as well.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's climactic hope in verses 10-11?

options.text: That God will not abandon his soul to Sheol nor let His Holy One see decay, and will show him the path of life and fullness of joy in His presence.
options.note: This is the psalm's highest point of hope, quoted by the apostles as messianic prophecy.

options.text: That David will avoid all suffering in his earthly life.
options.note: The psalm's hope concerns life beyond death, not the absence of earthly suffering.

options.text: That his descendants will inherit great wealth.
options.note: The psalm's climax concerns resurrection hope, not material inheritance for descendants.

options.text: That his enemies will be publicly humiliated.
options.note: This is not the psalm's focus in these verses, which center on personal hope beyond the grave.

quiz.q: Why is Psalm 16 significant for the earliest Christian preaching?

options.text: Both Peter at Pentecost and Paul at Pisidian Antioch quote verse 10 directly as scriptural proof of Christ's bodily resurrection.
options.note: This makes Psalm 16 one of the most explicitly messianic and apostolically confirmed prophetic texts in the Psalter.

options.text: It is quoted only once, briefly, with little theological weight given to it.
options.note: It is quoted at length in two major sermons, Acts 2 and Acts 13, each making it central to the argument for the resurrection.

options.text: It was primarily used by early Christians as a song of comfort with no doctrinal significance.
options.note: While it is comforting, its explicit doctrinal use by the apostles as resurrection proof is highly significant, not merely devotional.

options.text: It has no connection to the resurrection accounts in the Gospels or Acts.
options.note: This is directly contradicted by its prominent use in both Acts 2 and Acts 13.

questions: David says apart from God he has 'no good thing'. Where are you tempted to look for your ultimate good in something other than God, even something good in itself?

David calls the LORD his chosen portion and secure inheritance rather than land or wealth. What would change in your priorities this week if you truly held God, not your possessions or achievements, as your portion?
David sets the LORD always before him so that he will not be shaken. What practices help you keep God consciously before you in ordinary moments, not just in crisis?

This psalm's hope of resurrection was fulfilled specifically in Jesus, not in David himself. How does knowing Christ's resurrection is a settled historical fact, not just a future hope, change the way you face your own mortality?
The psalm ends with 'fullness of joy' and 'eternal pleasures' in God's presence. How does anticipating that promised joy shape the way you endure hardship or delayed gratification now?

translationNotes.note: Refuge renders chasah, the act of fleeing to God for shelter, and the psalm's opening posture of complete trust sets the tone for everything that follows.
Portion renders cheleq, drawn from the language of Israel's tribal land allotments; David applies this covenantal inheritance language directly to God Himself.

Holy One renders chasid, a title of covenant faithfulness; both Peter, Acts 2:27, and Paul, Acts 13:35, apply this verse directly to Christ, arguing that only His body, unlike David's, did not see decay.
